parameters.query:
WITH run AS (
  SELECT domain_id
  FROM runs
  WHERE id = $1::bigint
)
-- The first node after the trigger, and the shape the parent design fixes for every
-- workflow in this set (.specs/2026-08-19-research-pipeline-port.md, section 4): the
-- domain's personas and taxonomy, read as ONE query answering exactly one row. Both
-- halves of that are claims about this statement rather than house style, and both
-- are readable off it.

-- ONE QUERY, because the alternative is a lookup node per list, and a lookup node is
-- a second branch that races whatever reads it. What is fetched is small by
-- construction: a domain's personas, categories, terms and criteria are rows an
-- operator wrote, so taking them together costs one round trip and nothing else.

-- ONE ROW, because a Postgres node maps its statement over the items it was handed
-- and passes on what the statement returned. A SELECT matching nothing returns no
-- row, the node emits no item, and every node below it is then skipped with nothing
-- written anywhere: the pass ends looking exactly like a pass that found no work.
-- That is the failure this shape exists to make impossible. The outer SELECT names
-- no FROM at all, so it produces one row whatever the database holds, and every list
-- is a scalar subquery COALESCEd to an empty JSON array.

-- Which leaves one thing for every node below to be careful about. An empty list
-- here is a measured empty, an unresolvable run is not, and the two arrive spelled
-- the same way. domain_id is the discriminator and the only one: NULL when the run
-- id matched no row, a real id when the domain simply states no terms. Read it
-- before reading a length.

-- run_id is the parameter rather than a column read back, so it survives a run id
-- that resolves to nothing. It has to travel because this node's answer REPLACES the
-- item the trigger was handed: whatever the dispatcher sent is gone past here, and
-- the run is what a ledger row and the closing update are charged to.

-- Every list is ordered, which nothing downstream requires and every reader benefits
-- from: two passes over one unchanged domain hand the nodes below the same lists in
-- the same order, so a diff between two runs is about the documents rather than
-- about the order a planner happened to return rows in.
SELECT
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  (SELECT domain_id FROM run) AS domain_id,

  -- The domain row, cut to the members the nodes below read. feature_version is the
  -- one that has to travel: the feature group holds each document's composed version
  -- against the domain's, and fetching one integer separately is the lookup node
  -- this shape exists to avoid. NULL rather than an empty object when the run id
  -- resolved to nothing, which is the same discriminator domain_id carries.
  (SELECT jsonb_build_object(
     'id', d.id,
     'slug', d.slug,
     'name', d.name,
     'settings', d.settings,
     'feature_version', d.feature_version,
     'embedding_model', d.embedding_model)
     FROM domains d
    WHERE d.id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)) AS domain,

  -- The personas. system_text is operator-owned prose and is the trusted half of
  -- what prompt-frame.ts composes around an untrusted chunk; nothing in this
  -- workflow writes it, and no node below may put a document's text where a persona
  -- belongs.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', p.id,
       'role', p.role,
       'system_text', p.system_text)
       ORDER BY p.role, p.id)
       FROM personas p
      WHERE p.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS personas,

  -- The categories, which are the buckets the terms below are filed under. key
  -- rather than id is what a reader downstream matches on: features.ts builds a
  -- column name out of it and static-gate.ts groups hits by it, so the surrogate
  -- id travels for an operator's benefit and the key is what the libraries read.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', c.id,
       'key', c.key,
       'name', c.name,
       'parent_id', c.parent_id)
       ORDER BY c.key, c.id)
       FROM categories c
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS categories,

  -- The terms, joined to their category's key rather than carrying category_id.
  -- Four members and this exact spelling, because three libraries read this one
  -- list and each reads a different subset of it: static-gate.ts takes pattern,
  -- weight and polarity, features.ts takes pattern and category, and
  -- feature-version.ts takes all four. A term list selected without the join
  -- satisfies the first reader and starves the other two, with nothing failing.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'category', c.key,
       'pattern', t.pattern,
       'weight', t.weight,
       'polarity', t.polarity)
       ORDER BY c.key, t.pattern, t.id)
       FROM terms t
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = t.category_id
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS terms,

  -- The criteria, joined to their category the same way. Nothing in this workflow
  -- reads them: they are ar-score's subject, and ar-score is invoked with a run of
  -- its own and fetches its own context. They are selected here because the design
  -- fixes the taxonomy as what this node fetches, and the taxonomy is these three
  -- tables, so a node group added below reads them without a second lookup and
  -- without a second branch to reason about.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', k.id,
       'category', c.key,
       'value', k.value,
       'kind', k.kind)
       ORDER BY c.key, k.kind, k.id)
       FROM criteria k
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = k.category_id
      WHERE k.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM run)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS criteria

SELECT
-- One row per source, and every node group below this one is built on that. A
-- Postgres node maps its statement over the items it was handed and passes on what
-- the statement returned, so this node takes the one context item above it and
-- answers as many items as the domain has sources worth reading. An HTTP Request node
-- runs once per input item, so a pass over four sources makes four requests because
-- this statement answered four rows, and nothing below it has to loop.

-- Which also means this node's answer REPLACES the context item, the way that item
-- replaced the one the trigger was handed. The personas and the taxonomy are not
-- gone, but they are no longer in $json: a node below reaches them as $('Load Domain
-- Context').first().json, for the same reason ar-dispatch's Invoke Target Workflow
-- reads its workflow id off Plan Dispatch rather than off the item the Postgres node
-- in front of it wrote. run_id is the exception and is echoed into every row from the
-- parameter, because a ledger row and a closing update are charged to the run rather
-- than to a source.

-- Two parameters, in declaration order: the run and the domain, both read off that
-- one item. Neither is asked of the database again here. The pair came out of a
-- single read of the runs row a moment ago, so a second lookup would re-read a row
-- nothing has changed, and deriving the domain a second way is how the two start
-- being able to disagree.

-- One SELECT over one table, and that is a property of this schema rather than of the
-- statement. The design this one is ported from held a feed's configuration in a
-- hand-written module and its cursor in a table of its own, so the equivalent read
-- joined what a person had edited to what a run had written, and adding a feed meant
-- a deploy. Here everything that varies per feed is a column on the row: the whole of
-- a source is one row, and this is the whole of the selection.

-- Eleven of the twelve columns, and enabled is the omission. It is the WHERE clause's
-- business rather than a reader's below: a row that reached this projection is
-- enabled by construction, and carrying the column onward is an invitation to branch
-- on it a second time.

  $1::bigint AS run_id,

  -- Which feed this is and how to reach it. kind is what selects the adapter for the
  -- row, and the two ids are what a document written from this source is filed under.
  -- endpoint is NOT NULL and may still be empty, which is a source somebody has not
  -- finished configuring rather than one that needs no address.
  s.id AS source_id,
  s.domain_id,
  s.kind,
  s.endpoint,

  -- The arrangement, from both of its ends: how to read this source, and what a
  -- correct reading of it looks like. Data the parse engine is directed by, and never
  -- anything it evaluates, which is what keeps adding a feed an INSERT. Both default
  -- to an empty object, so a source nobody has configured yet arrives here shaped
  -- like every other one and the adapter's own defaults apply.
  s.parser_config,
  s.contract,

  -- Where the last fetch stopped, in whatever spelling the adapter that wrote it
  -- chose. NULL means this source has never been fetched, or that its adapter keeps
  -- no cursor at all. It stays NULL rather than becoming an empty string, which an
  -- adapter would hand back to its source as a real position.
  s.cursor,

  -- The four members src/lib/source-health.ts reads, selected here so the health node
  -- group can work a source's next counters out of the item it already holds rather
  -- than out of a second SELECT. flagged is in that list even though the WHERE clause
  -- below has already fixed it at false: reading it off the row keeps the library's
  -- input a reading, where a Code node restating the constant would be this
  -- statement's own predicate written down a second time, somewhere it can stop
  -- agreeing.
  s.consecutive_failures,
  s.last_success_at,
  s.last_failure_at,
  s.flagged
FROM sources s
-- enabled AND NOT flagged, and the sticky note beside this node carries the argument
-- for why those are two columns rather than one. What belongs on the statement is
-- that both are NOT NULL with a default, so this predicate partitions the domain's
-- sources rather than quietly dropping the rows whose flag was never set: a nullable
-- boolean compares UNKNOWN, and a row that is neither selected nor excluded is the
-- one nobody goes looking for.
WHERE s.domain_id = $2::bigint
  AND s.enabled
  AND NOT s.flagged
-- A NULL domain_id selects nothing, which is where a pass started by hand ends: no
-- request is made and no row is written anywhere. Three different situations reach
-- zero rows here and this statement parts none of them, those being no run behind the
-- id, a domain with no sources, and a domain whose sources are all switched off or
-- flagged. domain_id on the context item is the discriminator, which is why Load
-- Domain Context answers one row whatever the database holds and this node does not
-- have to.

-- Ordered by id, which nothing below requires and every reader benefits from, for the
-- reason the lists in the node above are ordered: two passes over one unchanged
-- domain hand the nodes below the same sources in the same order.
ORDER BY s.id

WITH
-- Where a reading becomes a row, and the keep half of fail-flag-keep written as one
-- statement. A reading its contract refused is stored with the reason it was refused
-- rather than dropped, so a source whose shape has moved leaves evidence behind
-- instead of a fall in volume that reads exactly like a quiet week.

-- Extract Records decided the parse and nothing here revisits it. parse_status and
-- parse_error arrive as parameters and are written as they came: the contract was
-- read up there, beside the config that directed the reading, and a second judgment
-- down here would be a copy with nothing comparing it against the first.

-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever happened. The insert sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT names
-- no FROM, so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was handed. A
-- reading that was written, a repeat capture that was not, and an item carrying no
-- reading at all each answer one row, which is what lets the health group below pair
-- its input against Extract Records by index, the same pairing Extract Records makes
-- against the fetch. Select Active Sources is reached differently, its rows being one
-- per source where these items are one per reading: the health group gathers the
-- readings under the source id each of them carries. An INSERT ... RETURNING on its
-- own emits nothing for a conflict, and the item would then vanish from the stream at
-- exactly the point where a repeat capture is the ordinary outcome.

-- Seven parameters, in declaration order: the run, the domain, the source, the
-- reading, the entry it was read from, and the two columns the parse answered. The
-- two JSONB members travel as the text JSON.stringify made of them, because the
-- payload of a url or an rss source is one whole document rather than an object, and
-- a bare string is not JSON until something encodes it.

-- The whitespace run the hash basis collapses, spelled out rather than left to the
-- shorthand class. Postgres reads that shorthand as ASCII whitespace and JavaScript
-- reads it, under the u flag, as the Unicode set, so the two disagree about a
-- non-breaking space and about a byte order mark sitting inside a body.
-- src/sources/listing-api.ts computes the same digest Node side and both writers
-- share one unique key, so a class differing by a single code point is two rows for
-- one item on every source that is reached both ways.
whitespace AS (
  SELECT '[\u0009\u000a\u000b\u000c\u000d\u0020\u00a0\u1680'
      || '\u2000\u2001\u2002\u2003\u2004\u2005\u2006\u2007'
      || '\u2008\u2009\u200a\u2028\u2029\u202f\u205f\u3000'
      || '\ufeff]+' AS run
),

-- The parameters, cast once. Both JSONB members arrive as JSON text, so a JavaScript
-- null arrives as the JSON null literal rather than as SQL NULL, and nullif is what
-- puts the two absences back together. documents.raw draws that distinction in its
-- own comment: NULL says no payload was ever stored, where a JSON null would claim
-- the source answered and answered with nothing.
candidate AS (
  SELECT
    $2::bigint AS domain_id,
    $3::bigint AS source_id,
    nullif($4::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS record,
    nullif($5::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS raw,
    $6::text AS parse_status,
    $7::text AS parse_error
),

-- The two columns a documents row takes from the reading, read off the field map by
-- name. url and body are the field names both adapters under src/sources/ write, and
-- that convention is the whole of the mapping: naming a field map's members after the
-- columns costs an operator one sentence of documentation, where a second mapping
-- from field names to column names would be another config to get wrong, and getting
-- it wrong would produce documents with no body and nothing to say why.

-- A member that is not a string is not text whatever it coerced to, so a numeric url
-- reads as no url rather than as a link to a number. The empty string is an absence
-- for url, which is NULL where there is no such place and never '', and a value for
-- body, which is NOT NULL and may still be empty: a capture that yielded no text was
-- kept anyway, which is the rule this whole statement is named after.

-- The WHERE clause is what confines this statement to readings. An item carrying no
-- record is a source that answered nothing on this pass, and that is a fact about the
-- source rather than a document: nothing is inserted, the outer SELECT still answers
-- its one row, and the health group below is what records that the fetch happened and
-- came back with nothing to read. What that costs is the payload, which reaches no
-- column and does not survive the pass. Storing it would put rows in the corpus that
-- no reader of the corpus wants, since every one of them treats a row as an item that
-- was captured rather than as a fetch that was attempted.
reading AS (
  SELECT
    c.domain_id,
    c.source_id,
    c.raw,
    c.parse_status,
    c.parse_error,
    nullif(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(c.record -> 'url') = 'string'
                THEN c.record ->> 'url'
           END, '') AS url,
    COALESCE(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(c.record -> 'body') = 'string'
                  THEN c.record ->> 'body'
             END, '') AS body
  FROM candidate c
  WHERE c.record IS NOT NULL
),

-- The content hash, and the key one row per distinct item stands on. The basis is the
-- url and the body, each with its whitespace runs collapsed and its ends trimmed,
-- JSON encoded into a two member array so that the halves cannot bleed into each
-- other: without the encoding a url ending in the first words of a body would collide
-- with a shorter url and a longer one.

-- What is left OUT of the basis is the half that does the work. The source is not in
-- it, deliberately, because documents.hash exists so that capturing the same item
-- from a second source lands on the row already there rather than beside it. Neither
-- is the run, nor the day, nor the domain.

-- Byte for byte the digest src/sources/listing-api.ts computes, and the agreement is
-- measured rather than asserted: the same hash over the same JSON encoding of the
-- same collapsed pair. Nothing fails when the two drift apart. The corpus doubles
-- instead.
hashed AS (
  SELECT
    r.domain_id,
    r.source_id,
    r.raw,
    r.parse_status,
    r.parse_error,
    r.url,
    r.body,
    encode(sha256(convert_to(
      '[' || to_json(collapsed.url)::text
          || ',' || to_json(collapsed.body)::text || ']',
      'UTF8')), 'hex') AS hash
  FROM reading r
  CROSS JOIN whitespace ws
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT
      btrim(regexp_replace(COALESCE(r.url, ''), ws.run, ' ', 'g'), ' ') AS url,
      btrim(regexp_replace(r.body, ws.run, ' ', 'g'), ' ') AS body) AS collapsed
),

-- The write. DO NOTHING is what makes a repeat capture write no second row, and the
-- conflict target is the constraint by NAME rather than the column list, so renaming
-- the constraint breaks this statement instead of quietly arbitrating on something
-- else. documents.hash carries the argument for why the column is NOT NULL as well as
-- UNIQUE: a nullable member would leave this clause never firing at all, with the
-- insert reporting success and the corpus gaining a copy per pass.

-- parse_status is written rather than left to its default. The column defaults to ok
-- and its own comment says exactly what that default cannot tell apart, being a
-- document that parsed from one whose writer never set the column. This writer always
-- knows which, so it says which, and a NULL reaching here is Extract Records
-- contradicting itself rather than an absence for a default to fill. NOT NULL is what
-- reports it, loudly, which is the right volume for a state that cannot happen.

-- What a repeat capture does NOT do is correct the row already standing. The stored
-- row keeps the first reading's status and its error. Content that hashes the same
-- cannot have diverged differently unless the contract itself moved, and moving a
-- contract is an operator's edit whose re-parse is a pass of its own rather than
-- something to smuggle in behind a dedupe.
written AS (
  INSERT INTO documents (
    domain_id, source_id, hash, url, body, raw, parse_status, parse_error)
  SELECT
    h.domain_id, h.source_id, h.hash, h.url, h.body, h.raw,
    h.parse_status, h.parse_error
  FROM hashed h
  ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT documents_hash_unique DO NOTHING
  RETURNING id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, and it is about the write rather than about the parse.
-- The reading, its warnings, the config faults and the HTTP status all stay on
-- Extract Records' items, which the health group reads back by name and a node below
-- can too. Restating any of them in this projection would be a second copy able to
-- disagree with the first, and the three ids below are here because a ledger row and
-- the closing update are charged to the run rather than to a source.

-- document_id is the row this reading is in, whether or not this pass is what put it
-- there. COALESCE reads it out of the insert when there was one and out of the corpus
-- when there was not, and only one of the two can ever answer: the outer query reads
-- the snapshot this statement began under, so it cannot see the row the CTE above
-- just wrote. NULL means there is no document, which is the item that carried no
-- reading.

-- document_inserted is the other half of that pair and the two answer different
-- questions. A repeat capture is a fetch that worked and wrote nothing, so a reader
-- counting new material reads this flag while a reader following a document reads the
-- id, and neither has to infer its answer from the other.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  $2::bigint AS domain_id,
  $3::bigint AS source_id,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT n.id FROM written n),
    (SELECT d.id FROM documents d JOIN hashed h ON h.hash = d.hash)) AS document_id,
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM written) AS document_inserted

WITH
-- Where four values become four columns, and the fail and flag halves of
-- fail-flag-keep written as one statement. Judge Source Health decided them and
-- nothing here revisits the decision: the counter, the two stamps and the flag arrive
-- as parameters and are written as they came. src/lib/source-health.ts holds the
-- arithmetic, the node above is where the outcome was read off this pass's readings,
-- and a rule restated down here would be a copy with nothing comparing it against the
-- first.

-- BOTH STAMPS EVERY PASS, including the one that did not move. The answer above holds
-- four values and this statement is built from exactly those, so the stamp being
-- carried through is written back as it came. Writing only the one that moved would
-- mean working out down here which of them did, which is the decision taken a second
-- time in a second language. What the round trip costs is precision and nothing else:
-- the column holds microseconds and the item carried the value as JSON, so a
-- carried-through stamp is rewritten at the millisecond it survived as. Whether a
-- source is broken right now is read off which of the two stamps is the more recent,
-- and a millisecond parts no two passes.

-- Six parameters, in declaration order: the run, the source, the counter, the two
-- stamps and the flag. A stamp the node above could not read as one arrives here as
-- it came and the cast refuses it, loudly, which is the right volume: a NULL written
-- in its place would claim the source has never once succeeded.

-- The write is blind and keyed on the id. The values it applies were worked out from
-- a row read at the top of this pass, so two passes reaching one source at the same
-- time would have the later write win and lose the earlier one's bump. Nothing here
-- locks the row, and what keeps passes apart is a claim taken much further up:
-- ar-dispatch selects a due topic FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and pushes next_run_at
-- forward before it invokes anything, so one topic is in flight once. A domain
-- carrying two topics is what that claim does not cover, and the cost there is a
-- counter short by one rather than a wrong flag, both passes having read the same
-- source and agreed about how it answered.
applied AS (
  UPDATE sources
  -- FOUR COLUMNS AND NO FIFTH. enabled is not in this list and may not be. It is the
  -- operator's column outright, where flagged is the pipeline's own reading, and
  -- src/db/schema/sources.ts keeps the two apart so the rot detector cannot switch
  -- off a feed somebody deliberately turned on. The library answers exactly the four
  -- written here and carries no enabled member for the same reason: a column named in
  -- an answer is a column somebody eventually writes.

  -- flagged is set here and never cleared here, which is a property of the value
  -- rather than of this clause. The library sets it once the counter reaches the
  -- threshold and has no member that unsets it, so this statement can write false
  -- only for a source that was already false. Clearing a flag is an operator's act,
  -- taken once whatever broke has been fixed.
  SET
    consecutive_failures = $3::integer,
    last_success_at = $4::timestamptz,
    last_failure_at = $5::timestamptz,
    flagged = $6::boolean
  WHERE id = $2::bigint
  RETURNING consecutive_failures, flagged
)

SELECT
-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever happened. The update sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT names
-- no FROM, so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was handed. An
-- UPDATE ... RETURNING on its own emits nothing when its WHERE matches nothing, and
-- the source would then drop out of the stream at the one point where its absence is
-- worth reporting.

-- health_applied is that case named. False means the row this pass read at the top is
-- no longer there, which is a source deleted mid pass rather than a source that
-- failed, and counting the two as one thing is how a deletion turns into a flag
-- nobody can explain.

-- The counter and the flag are read back out of the update rather than echoed from
-- the parameters, so what this node answers is what the row now holds. Nothing else
-- is restated: the readings, their warnings, the config faults and the HTTP status
-- stay on Extract Records' items, where a node below reaches them by name.

-- A pass that succeeded is a counter of 0, and no separate member says so. The
-- library resets to a real zero on a success and to nothing else, and the threshold
-- it compares against is a positive integer, so the two readings are one reading. A
-- member saying it again would be a copy able to disagree with the column beside it.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  $2::bigint AS source_id,
  (SELECT a.consecutive_failures FROM applied a) AS consecutive_failures,
  (SELECT a.flagged FROM applied a) AS flagged,
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM applied) AS health_applied

WITH
-- Where the corpus a new document is held against is read, and the only node in this
-- group that touches the database. The two Code nodes below it cannot: a spliced
-- library imports nothing and a Code node opens no connection, so the corpus arrives
-- here as data or the dedupe below has nothing to hold anything against.

-- ONE READ FOR THE PASS. executeOnce is set on this node, so it runs against the
-- first item it was handed and answers once. What it selects is a fact about the
-- domain rather than about a source, and Apply Source Health above answers one item
-- per source, so without the setting this statement would run once per source and
-- hand the node below the same corpus over again for each of them. Nothing downstream
-- reads past the first item either way: Mark Near Duplicates takes the first and
-- nothing else, so the setting costs round trips rather than meaning.

-- Two parameters, in declaration order: the run and the domain. The domain is read
-- back off Load Domain Context by name rather than off the item this node was handed,
-- Apply Source Health's projection carrying a source and no domain. The run travels
-- for the reason it travels everywhere on this canvas: a ledger row and the closing
-- update are charged to it and not to a source.
recent AS (
  -- The window, and it is a ROW CAP rather than a span of time. What a dedupe needs
  -- is enough recent material to recognise a repeat in, and how much material that is
  -- depends on how fast a domain moves: a span of days gives a quiet domain almost
  -- nothing to compare against and a busy one more than a pass can sketch. A cap on
  -- rows gives both the same window and lets the domain decide how long it reaches
  -- back.

  -- What the cap costs is said rather than hidden. An item near enough to a document
  -- older than the two hundredth most recent one is not recognised here, and the
  -- exact key in Write Documents is what still catches it when the bytes agree. Two
  -- hundred is a bound on the sketching this pass does rather than a claim about how
  -- long a repeat stays interesting.

  -- Every document of the domain, and neither exclusion a reader expects is made. The
  -- rows this pass just wrote are in the window because they are in the corpus, and
  -- the node below parts a document from itself by id rather than by when a row
  -- arrived. A document whose reading its contract refused is in it too: its body is
  -- content that was captured, and content arriving twice is what this window is for
  -- whatever a contract made of it.
  SELECT d.id, d.body
  FROM documents d
  WHERE d.domain_id = $2::bigint
  ORDER BY d.id DESC
  LIMIT 200
)

SELECT
-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever the domain holds. The corpus is a scalar subquery COALESCEd
-- to an empty array and the outer SELECT names no FROM, so this node answers exactly
-- one item however few documents there are to put in it. A domain with nothing in the
-- corpus yet answers an empty array, which the node below reads as nothing to compare
-- against rather than as a node that did not run.

-- A NULL domain_id selects nothing and reaches the same empty array. That is a pass
-- started by hand rather than by the dispatcher, and Load Domain Context is where the
-- two are told apart.

-- The array is ordered ASCENDING by id while the window above takes the newest rows
-- descending, and the two orders are doing different jobs. The window is about which
-- documents to carry; the order is about which of several converging members a
-- document is marked against, and the node below stops at the first it converges
-- with. Ascending makes that the earliest, which is the row a person following a
-- duplicate back wants to land on.

-- Two members per entry and no more. The id is what orders a pair and what a mark
-- names, the body is what a sketch is built from, and everything else about a
-- document is a question for the table. A hash is deliberately not here: exact
-- repetition was settled in Write Documents, and this window exists for the pairs
-- that key cannot see.
  $1::bigint AS run_id,
  $2::bigint AS domain_id,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', r.id, 'body', r.body)
       ORDER BY r.id)
       FROM recent r),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS corpus

## Invoked, Never Scheduled

This workflow starts when `ar-dispatch` reaches it through Invoke Target Workflow, and the Execute Workflow Trigger on this canvas is the whole of what makes that possible. It holds no clock and may not acquire one: `ar-dispatch` carries the only Schedule Trigger in the system, and `tests/invariants/workflows.test.ts` counts them across every built workflow and names the one file allowed to hold one.

Scheduling this workflow is a row instead. A `topics` row says how often a domain should be pulled and when it is next due, the dispatcher claims it once `next_run_at` has passed, and this workflow is invoked for the claim. So changing the cadence is an UPDATE rather than an edit to this canvas.

### What arrives, and what does not

One item carrying `run_id`, and nothing else. `Open Run` opens the `runs` row before the invocation and its `RETURNING` projection is the item forwarded here, so the claimed topic does not survive the hop: what this workflow knows about the pass it is running is the run, and the domain is read back off that. `Load Domain Context` is where that happens.

The trigger is typeVersion 1, which passes the caller's item through as it stands. Nothing here declares an input schema, so what the dispatcher sends is what the first node reads, and adding a schema later is a change to both ends rather than to this node alone.

### Started by hand

A run started from this canvas rather than by the dispatcher carries no `run_id`, and nothing pretends otherwise. `Load Domain Context` answers a null `domain_id` and four empty lists, which is a shape a node below can refuse by name. It is not an error worth suppressing: a pass with no run to charge has nowhere to write what it did.

## Flagged Is Not Disabled

Two columns keep a source out of this pass, and they are not one column written twice. `Select Active Sources` reads both: `enabled AND NOT flagged`.

`flagged` is the pipeline's own reading, and the flag half of fail-flag-keep. `src/lib/source-health.ts` decides it: handed a source's counters and one fetch outcome, it answers a `flagged` of true once `consecutive_failures` has reached the threshold. Skipping the row is what makes setting the flag worth anything. A rotted feed that goes on being fetched spends a request every pass, stores payloads nothing can read, and buries the sources still worth reading underneath them.

Nothing on this canvas clears it. `source-health.ts` sets the flag and has no member that unsets it, and `Apply Source Health` writes back exactly what it was answered, so a `false` reaches the column only for a source whose flag was already false. A flag the same automation could clear is a source that alternates quietly between working and not with nobody told, and the repair is usually a new `parser_config`, which is a pending row and an approval of its own. Clearing it is an operator's act, taken once what broke has been fixed.

### Switching a source off is a column of its own

`enabled` is the operator's outright, and the two are separate because they answer different questions. `flagged` says the pipeline believes this feed has stopped working; `enabled` says whether it may be read at all. Collapsing them would let the detector switch off a feed an operator deliberately turned on, and leave nowhere to record a suspect source still worth reading.

### What a skipped source costs

Nothing on this pass and nothing after it. A source this node does not select produces no item, so nothing is requested for it, no document is written under it, and its counter and its two stamps stay where the last pass left them. Which sources a domain is skipping is a question for the table, and the rows are the answer.

A domain whose sources are all switched off or flagged selects nothing at all, and the chain below is skipped whole. The `runs` row still closes: `ar-dispatch` opened it and waits for this workflow to return, so a pass with nothing to fetch ends looking like the pass it was.

## One Request Per Source

`Fetch Source Payload` runs once for every item `Select Active Sources` answered, so that statement's row count is this pass's request count and nothing here loops. A source is reached once per pass, and paging across passes is what the cursor is for.

### The cursor travels as a query parameter

`sources.cursor` is opaque text: only the adapter that wrote it has to understand it, and this node does not read it at all. It is sent under whatever name `parser_config.cursor_param` gives, and a source naming none sends no cursor. There is no default name, because guessing one puts a parameter nobody asked for on every request, where a source ignoring it looks exactly like a source honouring it.

A NULL cursor sends nothing either. The column stores an absence rather than an empty string, and an empty string handed back to a source is a real position.

What that does not serve is a cursor an API takes as a header, an entity tag being the usual one. `src/sources/paged-list.ts` sends those Node side, over an endpoint list one row cannot hold. Serving one here would be another `parser_config` key and another expression, never a branch on what a cursor happens to look like.

### Nothing here ends the pass

`fullResponse` is on, so this node answers exactly one item per request whatever the body turned out to be. Without it a JSON array comes back as one item per element, and the node below could no longer say which source a payload came from.

`neverError` is on, so a 404 or a 500 arrives as data carrying its status, and the error output continues on the regular branch, so a refused connection, a timeout or an endpoint somebody never finished configuring arrives as an item carrying no status at all. Each of those is an outcome a source can have and each is the health group's to read. A dead source is a row to flag, not a pass to abort.

## One Row Per Distinct Item

`Write Documents` inserts one `documents` row per reading and deduplicates on `documents.hash`, so capturing the same item twice writes once. Repetition is the ordinary case rather than a fault: a poll overlaps the one before it, two feeds carry the same item, an operator re-runs a pass by hand. All three land on the row already there.

The key is a digest over the item's own url and body and nothing else. The source is deliberately left out, which is what makes a second feed carrying an item land on the first feed's row instead of beside it, and the run is left out too, so re-running a pass costs requests and no rows.

### The same digest, computed twice

`src/sources/listing-api.ts` computes this hash Node side for the adapter path, and the statement on this node computes it in SQL for this one. Two writers, one unique key. Nothing raises when the two spellings drift apart: the corpus grows a second row for every item both paths reach, and the first symptom is a count somewhere much further downstream.

### What a repeat capture does not do

It does not correct the row already standing. The stored `parse_status` and `parse_error` are the first reading's, and content that hashes the same cannot have parsed differently unless the source's `contract` moved. Moving a contract is an operator's edit, and re-reading a corpus under a new one is a pass of its own rather than a side effect of the next poll.

### What is not a document

A fetch that yielded no reading writes nothing here. That covers a `parser_config` nobody can read, a payload holding no records where the config said records would be, and a request that never completed. Each is a fact about the source rather than an item in the corpus, and the health group beside this node is what records that it happened: the counter climbs, crossing the threshold sets `sources.flagged`, and the payload itself is not kept.

## The Free Decision Runs First

Two decisions are taken between a document being written and a model being asked about it, and both are free. `Mark Near Duplicates` says whether this pass captured something the domain already has, and `Gate Documents` says whether the domain's own terms make it worth reading. Neither opens a socket and neither writes a row.

The group below this one is where a pass starts costing something. Every document that reaches it went through here first, which is what makes the ordering on this canvas a spending rule rather than a preference.

### A duplicate is marked, not dropped

`documents.hash` already refuses an item captured twice byte for byte, so what is left here is the pair that reads the same and does not hash the same: a listing that re-renders, a page that gained a timestamp, one item carried by two feeds under different wrappers. `src/lib/shingle.ts` sketches both bodies and says whether they overlap enough to be one document.

A document that converges keeps its row and carries the id of the earlier one it matched. Nothing is merged and nothing is deleted, and only the earlier row goes on to be spent on. Which pair the pass thought were the same thing stays readable afterwards, which a merge would not leave behind.

### Two things a null means here

A document nothing could be compared against is not a document unlike everything else. `src/lib/shingle.ts` refuses to judge a body too short to fill a sketch, because overlap is measured against the smaller of two sketches and a short body would otherwise read as a perfect match for any longer one containing it. That refusal arrives as a null similarity beside a compared count of zero, never as a similarity of zero.

The gate draws the same line. A document with no body to score and one in a language the term set cannot read are both parked for a person with a null score, where a confident zero would drop them.

### What a domain with no terms gets

Every document ignored. The threshold is the library's default and a term set that matches nothing scores zero against it, so a domain nobody has written `terms` rows for spends nothing at all. That is the safe direction for a gate on spending, and each document says so: the reason recorded beside it carries the score, the threshold it was compared against and that no term matched.
